title: Austin A40 Farina: Italian design, British use
author: Les Caramagnols
excerpt: Introduced in 1958, the Austin A40 Farina combined an Austin base, Pininfarina styling and a more modern compact shape.
content:
The Austin A40 Farina arrived in 1958, at a time when BMC wanted to modernise the look of its small cars. It effectively replaced the A35 in the range without removing it immediately from the market, and it brought in styling by Pininfarina. For Austin, this was a way to make a popular car look sharper, more international and more current.

The model remained compact, but it was more than a styling update. It introduced a cleaner way of thinking about the small saloon, with crisper surfaces and, soon afterwards, a Countryman version with a split tailgate.

A popular Austin styled by Pininfarina

The A40 Farina is often remembered for its design. In the late 1950s, asking Pininfarina to shape a small Austin gave the car a different presence from rounder post-war British saloons. The lines were straighter, the volumes clearer and the car easier to read.

That restraint suited its use. The A40 was not a prestige car. It remained a compact model, powered by the A-Series family and built for ordinary service. The design brought freshness without changing the car's purpose.

The Countryman and a practical tailgate

The Countryman version soon introduced a two-piece tailgate. This made the little Austin much more flexible in use. It did not turn the A40 into a large estate car, but it made loading easier than with a conventional boot.

That is one of the model's strongest points. The A40 Farina stayed small while offering a practical solution that still makes sense to fans of compact classics.

MkII developments

The MkII, launched in the early 1960s, brought a longer wheelbase and changes to mechanical specification and appearance. The A-Series engine later gained capacity depending on version. These updates did not transform the car, but they made it more usable.

For buying or restoration, those differences matter. An A40 Farina should be identified by year, body style, engine, body condition and parts availability. Countryman versions add their own checks around the tailgate and water sealing.

A discreet but real place in the Austin range

The A40 Farina is not as famous as the Seven, the Mini or an Austin-Healey. It still matters because it shows BMC looking for a more European style for a mass-market car. Its career until 1967 confirms that it found a real place.

Identify before comparing

An old popular car is judged first by precise identity: generation, model year, market, engine, trim and state of preservation. Two cars that look close can require different parts, carry different equipment or have a different historical value.

For an Austin model, the useful reading starts with the period and the role in the range. A family saloon, a small popular car and a sporting derivative do not answer the same need, even when they share the same industrial background.

What matters on an example

The body is the first check. Sills, floors, wheelarches, door bottoms, mounting points and old repairs often say more than shiny paint. Simple mechanics can be repaired; a weakened shell becomes a serious project.

Any conclusion must therefore stay tied to the exact model, year and condition. Market, country, originality, parts availability and quality of previous work can change the practical answer. The technical frame gives direction, but the car itself gives the final evidence.
